prompt.context: One of our private equity clients recently acquired a leading European seafood restaurant chain. The chain owns and operates 700 restaurants across Europe. Same store sales (SSS) declined last year. The private equity parent has aggressive expectations for improved business performance.
prompt.question: How can the client improve same store sales (SSS)?

clarifying_info.q: What is driving the decline in same store sales?
How does our pricing and menu compare to competitors?
What are the current table configurations / seating arrangements?
clarifying_info.a: (Hand candidate Exhibit 3 — occupancy during peak hours)

exhibits.title: SSS Drivers Correlation Analysis
exhibits.shows: Three scatter plots showing correlation between SSS change (y-axis) and three potential drivers: unit price change (R²=0.04), number of items change (R²=0.04), and monthly traffic change (R²=0.82)

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmarking — Price, Bill Size, and Margin
exhibits.shows: Bar chart and table comparing the client against four competitor chains on average price per menu item (€), items per bill, and margin percentage

exhibits.title: Occupancy During Peak Hours (Candidate Copy)
exhibits.shows: Chart showing customer count by party size (1–6+) and table size (2, 4, 6, 8, 9+) during peak hours, with occupancy percentages up to 100%

framework: Decompose SSS into its drivers: customer traffic × average check size (price per item × number of items)
Use Exhibit 1 to identify which driver has the strongest correlation with SSS — traffic (R²=0.82) dominates; price and items have virtually no correlation (R²=0.04 each)
Assess ability to raise price or bill size using Exhibit 2 — client already priced at a premium, limited upside
Focus on increasing customer traffic — evaluate capacity, turnover, and seating optimization
Use Exhibit 3 to identify inefficiencies in table utilization during peak hours
Quantify bottom-line impact of a specific operational change (reconfiguring 4-seater tables)

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 1 tell you about the key driver of SSS, and what should the client focus on?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that customer traffic has a very high correlation with SSS (R²=0.82), while unit price change and number of items change have essentially no correlation (R²=0.04). Therefore the client should focus on initiatives that drive traffic or seat more customers, not on pricing or menu expansion.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 2 tell you about the client's pricing and competitive position?
questions.guidance: The client charges the highest average price per menu item (€10.95) and earns the highest margin (30%) among the five chains. Items per bill (4.4) is in the middle of the pack. This signals limited room to raise prices further — the client is already at a premium. Candidate should conclude that price/bill-size levers are largely exhausted.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 3 reveal about seating efficiency, and what opportunity does it present?
questions.guidance: The interviewer copy (not given to candidate) reveals that 4-seat tables are ~50% utilized during peak hours: roughly 1/4 of 4-seat tables have 3 occupants (75% occupancy) and 3/4 have 2 occupants (50% occupancy) → blended utilization ≈ 1/4×75% + 3/4×50% = ~56% ≈ 50%. On average only 2 people sit at a 4-seater. The opportunity is to reconfigure one 4-seater per restaurant into two 2-seaters, adding 2 seats and better matching actual party sizes.

math.setup: Average utilization of 4-seat tables during peak hours
steps: 1/4 of 4-seat tables occupied by 3 people → 75% seat utilization
3/4 of 4-seat tables occupied by 2 people → 50% seat utilization
Average people per 4-seat table: 4 seats × 50% utilization = 2 people
math.answer: 4-seat tables are roughly 50% utilized; only 2 people on average occupy a 4-top during peak hours

questions.prompt: What is the bottom-line annual profit impact of reconfiguring one 4-seater into two 2-seaters per restaurant?
questions.guidance: Candidate should work through the math step by step using the given/assumed inputs. Strong candidates will proactively build the model; good candidates will do so with some prompting.

math.setup: Reconfigure 1 four-top into 2 two-tops per restaurant → net +2 seats. Calculate additional meals per day, chain-wide revenue, and profit.
steps: Additional meals per restaurant per day: 2 seats × 2 peak hours × 2 turns = 8 meals
Total additional meals across chain: 8 × 700 restaurants = 5,600 meals
Additional revenue per day: 5,600 meals × €50 avg meal = €280,000

recommendation: The primary driver of SSS is customer traffic (R²=0.82); price and menu-item levers have near-zero correlation with SSS and are already stretched — the client is the highest-priced chain

The most actionable near-term opportunity is to reconfigure one 4-seat table per restaurant into two 2-seat tables, adding 2 seats that better match actual party sizes (average party = 2 people at a 4-top)
This seat-optimization initiative could deliver approximately €30M in additional annual profit with minimal capital investment
risks: Candidate should acknowledge the analysis is based on peak-hour data; off-peak impact may differ
Customer experience should be considered — smaller tables may affect dining comfort
Assumes table-turn rate and peak hours are stable and that demand exists to fill the added seats
next_steps: Pilot the table reconfiguration in a subset of restaurants to validate the uplift assumption
Investigate additional traffic-driving initiatives (marketing, loyalty programs, new dayparts) given that traffic is the key SSS lever
Monitor whether reconfiguration affects average check size or customer satisfaction
